title: What is Cloud Computing?
text:
Cloud computing is renting computers, storage, and services from a provider (like AWS, Google Cloud, Azure) over the internet instead of buying and maintaining your own physical hardware. Think of it like electricity — you don't build a power plant, you just plug in and pay for what you use.
Cloud Service Models

title: EC2 — Virtual Machines in the Cloud
text:
**EC2** (Elastic Compute Cloud) is AWS's virtual machine service. You can launch a server in seconds, choose the OS, configure the size (CPU, RAM), and pay only for the time it's running. Think of it as renting a computer by the hour.
EC2 Instance Lifecycle
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Pending: Launch instance
    Pending --> Running: Instance ready
    Running --> Stopping: Stop instance
    Stopping --> Stopped: Instance stopped
    Stopped --> Pending: Start instance
    Running --> ShuttingDown: Terminate
    ShuttingDown --> Terminated: Instance deleted
    Terminated --> [*]
EC2 CLI Commands
# Launch an EC2 instance
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0 \
  --instance-type t3.micro \
  --key-name my-key \
  --security-group-ids sg-12345 \
  --subnet-id subnet-67890

title: EC2 — Virtual Machines in the Cloud
text:
# List running instances
aws ec2 describe-instances --filters "Name=instance-state-name,Values=running"
# SSH into your instance
ssh -i my-key.pem ec2-user@<public-ip>
# Stop / Start / Terminate
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0
aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0
aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0

title: S3 — Object Storage
text:
**S3** (Simple Storage Service) stores files (called 'objects') in containers (called 'buckets'). It's designed for 99.999999999% durability (11 nines!) — meaning if you store 10 million files, you'd statistically lose 1 file every 10,000 years. It's used for static websites, backups, data lakes, and media storage.
S3 CLI Commands
# Create a bucket
aws s3 mb s3://my-company-assets-2024
# Upload a file
aws s3 cp backup.tar.gz s3://my-company-assets-2024/backups/
# Upload an entire directory
aws s3 sync ./public/ s3://my-company-assets-2024/website/
# List bucket contents
aws s3 ls s3://my-company-assets-2024/
# Download a file
aws s3 cp s3://my-company-assets-2024/backups/backup.tar.gz ./
# Delete a file
aws s3 rm s3://my-company-assets-2024/old-file.txt

title: S3 — Object Storage
text:
# Make a bucket public (for static websites)
aws s3 website s3://my-company-assets-2024 --index-document index.html
S3 Storage Classes (Cost Optimization)
Storage Class          Cost      Access            Use Case
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
S3 Standard            $$$      Instant            Frequently accessed data
S3 Infrequent Access   $$       Instant            Monthly backups
S3 Glacier Instant     $        Instant            Archive with rare access
S3 Glacier Flexible    ¢        Minutes-12 hours   Long-term archival
S3 Glacier Deep        ¢¢       12-48 hours        Compliance archives (7+ years)
info
S3 bucket names are globally unique across ALL AWS accounts. Use a naming convention like: company-environment-purpose (e.g., 'opsacademy-prod-assets'). Never put sensitive data in publicly accessible buckets!

VPC — Virtual Private Cloud
text:
A **VPC** is your own private network inside AWS. Think of it as building your own office complex in the cloud — you design the floor plan (subnets), install security doors (security groups), and decide which rooms have windows to the street (public subnets) vs. interior-only rooms (private subnets).
VPC Architecture

    IGW["🌐 Internet Gateway"] --> PUB1
    subgraph VPC ["VPC: 10.0.0.0/16"]
        subgraph PUB ["Public Subnet: 10.0.1.0/24"]
            PUB1["🌐 Load Balancer"]
            PUB2["🖥️ Bastion Host (SSH Jump)"]
        end
        subgraph PRIV ["Private Subnet: 10.0.2.0/24"]
            PRIV1["⚙️ App Servers"]

    style PUB fill:#162231,stroke:#10b98133,color:#e2e8f0

**Public Subnet** — Has a route to the Internet Gateway. Resources get public IPs. Used for load balancers and bastion hosts.
**Private Subnet** — No direct internet access. Used for application servers and databases. Can reach the internet through a NAT Gateway (outbound only).

title: VPC — Virtual Private Cloud
text:
**Security Groups** — Virtual firewalls attached to instances. Stateful: if you allow inbound traffic, the response is automatically allowed out.
**NACLs** — Network ACLs at the subnet level. Stateless: you must define both inbound and outbound rules.
tip
Interview architecture: 'I'd place the load balancer in a public subnet, app servers in a private subnet, and the database in an isolated private subnet with no internet access. The app servers reach the internet through a NAT Gateway for pulling updates.'

title: RDS and Lambda — Managed Services
text:
AWS offers managed services that handle the heavy lifting of running infrastructure. **RDS** manages your databases. **Lambda** runs your code without any servers at all.
Managed vs Self-Managed
graph LR
    subgraph SELF ["Self-Managed (EC2)"]
        A1["You manage EVERYTHING:\nOS patches, backups,\nscaling, monitoring,\nhigh availability"]
    end
    subgraph MANAGED ["Managed (RDS)"]
        B1["AWS manages:\nPatches, backups,\nreplicas, failover\nYou manage: Schema + queries"]
    end
    subgraph SERVERLESS ["Serverless (Lambda)"]
        C1["AWS manages:\nEVERYTHING\nYou manage: Just your code"]
    end
    style SELF fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style MANAGED fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style SERVERLESS fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
**RDS** (Relational Database Service) — Managed MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, or SQL Server. AWS handles backups, patching, replication, and failover. You just connect and run queries.

title: RDS and Lambda — Managed Services
text:
**Lambda** — Serverless compute. Upload your function code, and AWS runs it in response to events (API calls, S3 uploads, scheduled tasks). You pay only for the milliseconds your code runs. Zero servers to manage.
Lambda CLI Example
# Create a Lambda function
aws lambda create-function \
  --function-name process-order \
  --runtime nodejs18.x \
  --handler index.handler \
  --zip-file fileb://function.zip \
  --role arn:aws:iam::123456:role/lambda-role
# Invoke the function
aws lambda invoke --function-name process-order output.json
# View logs
aws logs tail /aws/lambda/process-order --follow
info
Lambda free tier: 1 million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds of compute per month — FREE forever. Perfect for microservices, API endpoints, image processing, and scheduled tasks.

title: Defensive Bash Scripting (set -euo pipefail)
text:
By default, Bash continues running a script even if a command fails! Imagine a backup script: `cd /backup_dir` fails (directory missing), and the next line is `rm -rf *`. Standard Bash will run `rm -rf *` inside your home directory and delete everything! Scared?
To prevent disaster, every professional production Bash script MUST start with the **Unofficial Bash Strict Mode**: `set -euo pipefail`.
Strict Mode Explanation
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
# -e : Exit immediately if ANY command returns a non-zero exit code
# -u : Exit immediately if an UNSET variable is referenced

title: Defensive Bash Scripting (set -euo pipefail)
text:
# -o pipefail : If any command in a pipeline fails (e.g. cat bad | grep foo), fail the WHOLE pipeline
tip
Interview favorite: 'What does set -euo pipefail do?' Explain each letter (-e, -u, -o pipefail). Mentioning this in any Linux/DevOps interview proves you have real-world production experience!

title: Error Trapping & Cleanup Hooks
text:
When a script crashes or exits, it might leave temporary files or lock files behind. The `trap` command registers a cleanup function that automatically executes whenever the script exits, dies, or receives a signal.
Bash Trap Cleanup Lifecycle
graph TD
    START["🚀 Script Begins"] --> TEMP["Create /tmp/lock.pid"]
    TEMP --> REG["trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM"]
    REG --> EXEC["Perform operations..."]
    EXEC -->|Script Exits or Crashes| TRAP["🧹 Trap Triggers: cleanup()"]
    TRAP --> RM["Delete /tmp/lock.pid"]
    RM --> FINISH["🏁 Clean Shutdown"]
    style TRAP fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style RM fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
Complete Robust Script Template
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
# Create temporary file
TEMP_FILE=$(mktemp /tmp/myapp.XXXXXX)
# Cleanup function
cleanup() {
  echo "Cleaning up temporary files..."
  rm -f "$TEMP_FILE"
}

title: Error Trapping & Cleanup Hooks
text:
# Register trap on EXIT, INT (Ctrl+C), TERM
trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM
echo "Processing data into $TEMP_FILE..."
# Do work here...

title: Argument Parsing ($1, $@, getopts)
Automated Disk & Log Monitoring Script
text:
One of the most common real-world interview coding tasks is: 'Write a script that monitors disk space and sends an alert if usage exceeds 80%.' Here is the production-grade implementation.
Disk Space Monitor Script
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
THRESHOLD=80
EMAIL="ops-alerts@company.com"
df -H | grep -vE '^Filesystem|tmpfs|cdrom' | awk '{ print $5 " " $1 }' | while read -r output; do
  usep=$(echo "$output" | awk '{ print $1}' | cut -d'%' -f1)
  partition=$(echo "$output" | awk '{ print $2 }')
if [ "$usep" -ge "$THRESHOLD" ]; then
    echo "[ALERT] Partition '$partition' is at $usep% usage on $(hostname) as of $(date)"
  fi
done

title: Explain 'set -euo pipefail' line by line.
text:
• `-e`: Abort script if any command fails (non-zero status)
• `-u`: Abort if an uninitialized variable is referenced
• `-o pipefail`: Pipeline returns failure status if ANY command in the pipeline fails

title: What is CI/CD?
text:
CI/CD is the practice of automating the entire software delivery process — from the moment a developer pushes code to the moment it's running in production. It's like an assembly line in a factory: code automatically goes through building, testing, and deploying without any manual steps.
CI/CD Pipeline Flow
graph LR
    A["👨‍💻 Developer\ngit push"] --> B["🔨 Build\nCompile code"]
    B --> C["🧪 Test\nUnit + Integration"]
    C --> D["📦 Package\nDocker image"]
    D --> E["🚀 Deploy Staging\nTest environment"]
    E --> F["✅ Deploy Production\nLive users"]
    style A fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style B fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style C fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
    style D fill:#1a2332,stroke:#8b5cf6,color:#e2e8f0
    style E fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style F fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0

title: What is CI/CD?
text:
**Continuous Integration (CI)** — Automatically build and test code every time someone pushes a commit. Catch bugs within minutes, not days.
**Continuous Delivery (CD)** — Automatically prepare releases that are ready to deploy at the push of a button.
**Continuous Deployment** — Go one step further: automatically deploy every change to production with no human intervention.
info
Without CI/CD, a team might deploy once a month with a scary 'big bang' release. With CI/CD, teams deploy multiple times per day with confidence — each change is small, tested, and easy to roll back.

title: GitHub Actions — Your First Pipeline
text:
**GitHub Actions** is GitHub's built-in CI/CD platform. Pipelines are defined as YAML files in `.github/workflows/` in your repository. Every push, pull request, or schedule can trigger a workflow.
GitHub Actions Concepts
graph TD
    WF["📋 Workflow\n(.github/workflows/ci.yml)"] --> JOB1["🔧 Job: Build\nruns-on: ubuntu-latest"]
    WF --> JOB2["🧪 Job: Test\nneeds: build"]
    WF --> JOB3["🚀 Job: Deploy\nneeds: test"]
    JOB1 --> S1["Step 1: Checkout code"]
    JOB1 --> S2["Step 2: Install deps"]
    JOB1 --> S3["Step 3: Build"]
    style WF fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style JOB1 fill:#162231,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style JOB2 fill:#162231,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
    style JOB3 fill:#162231,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
Your First GitHub Actions Workflow
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI Pipeline
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

title: GitHub Actions — Your First Pipeline
text:
- name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'
          cache: 'npm'
- name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci
- name: Run linter
        run: npm run lint
- name: Run tests
        run: npm test
- name: Build
        run: npm run build
tip
Use 'actions/checkout@v4' to clone your repo, 'actions/setup-node@v4' to install Node.js with caching. The 'cache: npm' option caches node_modules between runs, speeding up builds significantly.

title: Pipeline Stages — Build, Test, Deploy
text:
A well-designed pipeline has distinct stages that act as quality gates. Code must pass each stage before moving to the next. If any stage fails, the pipeline stops and the developer is notified.
Pipeline Stages with Quality Gates
graph LR
    A["📥 Code Push"] --> B{"🔨 Build"}
    B -->|Pass| C{"🧪 Unit Tests"}
    B -->|Fail ❌| STOP1["Notify Developer"]
    C -->|Pass| D{"🔗 Integration Tests"}
    C -->|Fail ❌| STOP2["Notify Developer"]
    D -->|Pass| E{"🔒 Security Scan"}
    D -->|Fail ❌| STOP3["Notify Developer"]
    E -->|Pass| F["📦 Build Docker Image"]
    F --> G["🚀 Deploy to Staging"]
    G --> H["✅ Deploy to Production"]
    style STOP1 fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style STOP2 fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style STOP3 fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style H fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
Multi-Stage Pipeline with Docker

title: Pipeline Stages — Build, Test, Deploy
text:
name: Full CI/CD Pipeline
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '18' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
build:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: docker build -t myapp:${{ github.sha }} .
      - name: Push to registry
        run: |
          echo ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }} | docker login -u ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }} --password-stdin
          docker push myapp:${{ github.sha }}
deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to production
        run: |
          echo "Deploying version ${{ github.sha }} to production..."
info

title: Pipeline Stages — Build, Test, Deploy
text: The 'needs' keyword creates dependencies between jobs. 'deploy needs: build' means deploy only runs after build succeeds. The 'if' condition ensures deploy only runs on the main branch, not on PRs.

title: Testing in CI/CD
text:
Testing is the backbone of CI/CD. Without automated tests, you're just automatically deploying bugs faster. The **testing pyramid** shows the optimal distribution of test types.
Testing Pyramid
graph TB
    E2E["🔝 E2E Tests\n(Few, slow, expensive)\nBrowser automation, full user flows"] 
    INT["🔷 Integration Tests\n(Medium count)\nAPI endpoints, database queries"]
    UNIT["🟢 Unit Tests\n(Many, fast, cheap)\nIndividual functions & components"]
    style E2E fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style INT fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style UNIT fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
**Unit Tests** — Test individual functions in isolation. Fast (milliseconds each). Run on every commit. Example: testing a `calculateDiscount()` function.
**Integration Tests** — Test how components work together. Example: testing that your API endpoint correctly reads from the database.

title: Testing in CI/CD
text:
**End-to-End (E2E) Tests** — Test the entire user flow in a real browser. Slow but catch real-world issues. Example: testing the full checkout flow.
Testing Matrix (Multiple Node Versions)
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: [16, 18, 20]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
      - name: Upload coverage
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v3
        if: matrix.node-version == 18
tip
Strategy matrix runs the same job with different configurations in parallel. Testing against Node 16, 18, and 20 simultaneously ensures your app works across all supported versions.

title: Environments and Secrets
text:
Production secrets (API keys, database passwords) should NEVER be hardcoded in your pipeline files or source code. CI/CD platforms provide encrypted secrets storage and environment-specific configurations.
Environment Promotion Flow
graph LR
    DEV["🛠️ Development\nEvery push"] -->|Auto| STAGING["🧪 Staging\nPre-production testing"]
    STAGING -->|Manual Approval| PROD["🚀 Production\nLive users"]
    style DEV fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style STAGING fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style PROD fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
Using Secrets in GitHub Actions
# Store secrets in: Settings → Secrets → Actions
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production       # Links to GitHub Environment
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to AWS
        env:
          AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}
          AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}
        run: |
          aws ecs update-service --cluster prod --service api --force-new-deployment

title: Environments and Secrets
text:
- name: Notify Slack
        run: |
          curl -X POST ${{ secrets.SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL }} \
            -d '{"text": "✅ Deployed to production!"}'
warning
Never echo, print, or log secrets in your pipeline! GitHub masks known secrets in logs, but custom formatting can accidentally expose them. Always use the ${{ secrets.NAME }} syntax — never hardcode.

title: Deployment Strategies
text:
How you deploy matters as much as what you deploy. Different strategies offer different tradeoffs between risk, speed, and complexity.
Deployment Strategies Comparison
graph TD
    subgraph RR ["Rolling Update"]
        R1["v1 v1 v1"] --> R2["v2 v1 v1"] --> R3["v2 v2 v1"] --> R4["v2 v2 v2"]
    end
    subgraph BG ["Blue-Green"]
        B1["Blue (v1) LIVE"] --> B2["Green (v2) Ready"]
        B2 --> B3["Switch traffic → Green LIVE"]
    end
    subgraph CN ["Canary"]
        C1["v1 (90% traffic)"] --> C2["v2 (10% traffic)"]
        C2 --> C3["v2 (100% traffic)"]
    end
    style RR fill:#0f1923,stroke:#00d4ff33,color:#e2e8f0
    style BG fill:#0f1923,stroke:#10b98133,color:#e2e8f0
    style CN fill:#0f1923,stroke:#f59e0b33,color:#e2e8f0
**Rolling Update** — Replace instances one by one. Zero downtime. Default in Kubernetes.

title: Deployment Strategies
text:
**Blue-Green** — Run two identical environments. Switch all traffic from Blue (old) to Green (new) instantly. Easy rollback: just switch back.
**Canary** — Route a small percentage of traffic (5-10%) to the new version. Monitor for errors. If healthy, gradually increase to 100%.
**Recreate** — Stop all old instances, then start new ones. Simple but causes downtime. Only for non-critical services.
tip
Interview answer: 'For critical production services, I use canary deployments — deploy to 5% of traffic, monitor error rates and latency for 15 minutes, then gradually promote to 100%. If metrics degrade, I automatically roll back. This limits the blast radius of any bad deployment.'

title: What is the difference between CI, CD (Delivery), and CD (Deployment)?
text:
**CI (Continuous Integration)**: Automatically build and test on every commit. Catch bugs early.

**CD (Continuous Delivery)**: Automatically prepare release artifacts. Needs manual approval to deploy.

**CD (Continuous Deployment)**: Fully automatic — every commit that passes tests goes straight to production. No human in the loop.

title: What are the 3 deployment strategies?
text:
1. **Rolling Update**: Replace pods one by one. Zero downtime. Default in K8s.
2. **Blue-Green**: Two environments. Switch traffic instantly. Easy rollback.
3. **Canary**: Send 5-10% traffic to new version. Monitor. Gradually increase.

Bonus: **Recreate** = stop old, start new (causes downtime).

title: What is the Testing Pyramid?
text:
Base (many): **Unit tests** — fast, test individual functions
Middle: **Integration tests** — test component interactions
Top (few): **E2E tests** — slow, test full user flows

Rule: More tests at the bottom (fast & cheap), fewer at the top (slow & expensive).

title: How do you handle secrets in CI/CD pipelines?
text:
NEVER hardcode secrets in code or YAML files!

Store in the CI platform's encrypted secrets store:
• GitHub: Settings → Secrets → Actions
• GitLab: Settings → CI/CD → Variables
• Jenkins: Credentials Manager

Access with: ${{ secrets.API_KEY }}

title: Linux Kernel Isolation: Seccomp, AppArmor & Capabilities
text:
### Defense in Depth in Linux Workloads
Containers share the host Linux kernel. Hardening the system call boundary is the primary defense against zero-day container breakout exploits:
```text
Container Application ──> [Seccomp (Syscall Filter)] ──> [AppArmor/SELinux (Path MAC)] ──> [Capabilities Filter] ──> Host Kernel
```
#### Security Layers:
1. **Seccomp (Secure Computing)**: Restricts which of the ~450 Linux system calls a process can make. Blocking calls like `ptrace`, `sys_chroot`, and `keyctl` neutralizes 90% of privilege escalation CVEs.
2. **Linux Capabilities**: Divides root privileges into granular sub-units (`CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`, `CAP_CHOWN`). Dropping all capabilities (`cap-drop: ALL`) and whitelisting only necessary ones prevents unauthorized packet sniffing or raw device access.

title: Linux Kernel Isolation: Seccomp, AppArmor & Capabilities
text: 3. **AppArmor / SELinux**: Mandatory Access Control (MAC) enforcing granular file read/write, network socket, and execution permissions.

title: Runtime Intrusion Detection with Falco & eBPF
text:
### eBPF-Powered Kernel Telemetry
**Falco** uses kernel instrumentation (via eBPF probes) to monitor system calls in real-time and trigger alerts when suspicious behavior occurs:
```yaml
- rule: Terminal Shell in Container
  desc: A terminal shell was spawned in a running production container
  condition: >
    spawned_process and container
    and proc.name in (bash, sh, zsh, dash)
  output: "Shell spawned in container (user=%user.name pod=%k8s.pod.name)"
  priority: WARNING
```
Unlike traditional log shippers, eBPF operates at the kernel ring buffer layer (<1% CPU overhead) and cannot be bypassed by user-space malware tampering with `/var/log`.

title: What is the difference between Seccomp and AppArmor?
text: Seccomp operates strictly at the system call level (filtering whether a syscall like ptrace or reboot is allowed). AppArmor operates at the file path and resource level (enforcing Mandatory Access Control on specific files, directories, and network sockets).

title: Why is running a container with ReadOnlyRootFilesystem considered a best security practice?
text: It prevents an attacker who exploits a web vulnerability from writing malicious binaries, rootkits, or persistence scripts to disk. Any required temporary scratch space is mounted explicitly via an ephemeral emptyDir volume.

title: How does eBPF improve container security observability over traditional kernel modules?
text: eBPF runs sandboxed bytecode verified by the Linux kernel in real time without modifying kernel source or inserting risky kernel modules. It provides low-overhead (<1%) tracing of all process events, socket traffic, and file accesses.

text:

**DevSecOps** moves security to the left ('Shift-Left'). Security testing happens automatically on every code commit inside the CI/CD pipeline, catching vulnerabilities within minutes while the code is fresh in the developer's mind.

title: OWASP Top 10 API Security Risks
text:
APIs are the primary gateway to your application's data. **OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project)** publishes the top 10 security vulnerabilities found in modern APIs. Every cloud engineer must know how to prevent them.
Top API Vulnerabilities Cheat Sheet

title: OWASP Top 10 API Security Risks
text:
Vulnerability                       Risk Explanation & Mitigation
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
API1: BOLA (Broken Object Level Auth) User A modifies URL /api/user/102 to access User B's data.
                                    Fix: Always check token userId == URL parameter ID!
API2: Broken Authentication          Weak JWT verification or missing expiration times.

title: 1. Scientific Forensic Process & Chain of Custody
text:
### What is Digital Forensics?
Digital forensics is the scientific process of preserving, identifying, extracting, documenting, and interpreting digital evidence so it can be used in legal proceedings, internal corporate investigations, or incident response.
According to IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report 2023, organizations with forensic-ready incident response teams contained breaches **54 days faster** — saving an average of **$1.49 million** per incident.
#### 5-Stage Scientific Methodology:
1. **Identification**: Locate all potential physical and cloud evidence sources.
2. **Preservation**: Protect original media with hardware write blockers and SHA-256 hashing.
3. **Acquisition**: Create byte-for-byte bitstream disk images (`.raw`, `.E01`) and RAM dumps (`.raw`, `.vmem`).

title: 1. Scientific Forensic Process & Chain of Custody
text:
4. **Analysis**: Reconstruct timeline, extract registry artifacts, and analyze unallocated space.
5. **Reporting**: Produce court-admissible, reproducible forensic reports.

title: 2. Memory Forensics with Volatility Framework
text:
### RAM Volatility Analysis
Volatile memory contains crucial ephemeral evidence: active process trees, injected DLLs, unencrypted network sockets, and plaintext passwords.
#### Volatility 3 Command Reference:
- **List Running Processes**: `vol -f memory.raw windows.pslist`
- **Detect Hidden/Injected Processes**: `vol -f memory.raw windows.pstree`
- **Extract Process Memory**: `vol -f memory.raw windows.dumpfiles --pid 1420`
- **Inspect Active Sockets**: `vol -f memory.raw windows.netscan`

title: 3. Disk Artifacts & Timeline Reconstruction
text:
### Windows & Linux Forensic Artifacts
- **Master File Table ($MFT)**: Metadata for every file on NTFS partitions.
- **Windows Registry**: User activity, auto-run persistence keys, recent documents.
- **Event Logs (`.evtx`)**: Security Event ID 4624 (Logon Success), 4625 (Logon Failed), 7045 (New Service Installed).
- **Prefetch (`.pf`)**: Proves execution timestamp and frequency of executable applications.

title: What is Chain of Custody and why is it essential in court?
text: Chain of Custody is the chronological paper trail or electronic log showing the seizure, custody, control, transfer, analysis, and disposition of digital evidence. Without a clear chain of custody, evidence can be ruled inadmissible in court due to potential tampering.

title: Why is a hardware write-blocker mandatory during disk acquisition?
text: Connecting a storage drive directly to an OS allows the OS to alter timestamps, write system metadata, or modify files. A hardware write-blocker prevents any write signals from reaching the evidence disk, guaranteeing a 100% byte-exact duplicate.

title: What Windows Event IDs are most critical during breach investigation?
text: Event ID 4624 (Logon Success), Event ID 4625 (Logon Failed), Event ID 4720 (User Account Created), Event ID 7045 (New Service Installed - common for malware persistence), and Event ID 1102 (Audit Log Cleared).

title: What are Containers?
text:
A container is a lightweight, standalone, executable package that includes everything needed to run a piece of software: code, runtime, system tools, libraries, and settings. Containers isolate applications from each other and from the host system.
Think of it like shipping containers in real life — a standardized box that can hold anything and be transported anywhere. Software containers work the same way: "Build once, run anywhere."

title: Docker Architecture
text:
Docker uses a client-server architecture. You type commands into the **Docker Client** (CLI), which sends HTTP API requests to the **Docker Daemon** (dockerd), which does the actual work of building, running, and managing containers.

**Image** — A read-only template containing your application code, runtime, libraries, and configuration. Think of it as a class in OOP.

title: Docker Architecture
text:
**Container** — A running instance of an image. Think of it as an object created from the class. You can have many containers from one image.
**Registry** — A storage service for Docker images. Docker Hub is the default public registry.
Essential Docker Commands

docker pull nginx              # Download an image from Docker Hub
docker images                  # List all local images
docker run nginx               # Create and start a container
docker run -d -p 80:80 nginx   # Run detached, map port 80

title: Building Images with Dockerfile
text:
A Dockerfile is a text file with instructions to build a Docker image. Each instruction creates a layer in the image, and Docker caches these layers for faster rebuilds. Think of it as a recipe — each step builds on the previous one.
Dockerfile Build Process
graph TD
    A["FROM node:18-alpine"] -->|Layer 1: Base image| B["WORKDIR /app"]
    B -->|Layer 2: Set directory| C["COPY package*.json ./"]
    C -->|Layer 3: Copy deps file| D["RUN npm install"]
    D -->|Layer 4: Install deps ⚡ CACHED| E["COPY . ."]
    E -->|Layer 5: Copy source code| F["CMD node server.js"]
    F --> G["🐳 Final Image"]

Example Dockerfile

title: Building Images with Dockerfile
text:
# Start from a base image
FROM node:18-alpine
# Set working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app
# Copy dependency files first (for caching)
COPY package*.json ./
# Install dependencies
RUN npm install --production
# Copy application code
COPY . .
# Expose port
EXPOSE 3000
# Define the command to run
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
tip
Interview tip: Copying package.json before the rest of the code is a Dockerfile best practice. If your code changes but dependencies don't, Docker reuses the cached npm install layer — saving minutes on each build.
Build and Run

docker build -t myapp:v1 .              # Build image, tag as myapp:v1
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 myapp:v1     # Run the container
docker image ls                         # List all images with sizes

text:
Real applications are never a single container. A typical web app might have: a frontend, a backend API, a database, and a cache. **Docker Compose** lets you define and run all these containers together with a single YAML file and a single command.

    environment:

    depends_on:
      - db

title: Multi-Stage Builds
text:
Multi-stage builds are a Dockerfile technique where you use multiple FROM statements to separate the **build environment** from the **runtime environment**. This dramatically reduces your final image size because build tools, compilers, and dev dependencies are left behind.
Multi-Stage Build Flow
graph LR
    subgraph STAGE1 ["Stage 1: Builder (1.2 GB)"]
        S1A["Node.js + npm"] --> S1B["Install ALL deps"]
        S1B --> S1C["Compile & Build"]
    end
    subgraph STAGE2 ["Stage 2: Production (85 MB)"]
        S2A["Alpine base only"] --> S2B["Copy built output"]
        S2B --> S2C["Production deps only"]
    end
    S1C -->|COPY --from=builder| S2B
    style STAGE1 fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style STAGE2 fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
Multi-Stage Dockerfile (React + Node.js)

title: Multi-Stage Builds
text:
# ---- Stage 1: Build ----
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci                      # Install ALL dependencies (including devDependencies)
COPY . .
RUN npm run build                # Compile React/TypeScript → static files
# ---- Stage 2: Production ----
FROM node:18-alpine AS production
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev            # Only production dependencies
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

title: Multi-Stage Builds
text:
The result: Your build stage might be 1.2 GB with all the compilers and dev tools. But the final production image is only 85 MB — containing just the compiled output and production runtime. This means faster deployments, smaller attack surface, and lower cloud costs.
info
Use 'npm ci' instead of 'npm install' in Dockerfiles. 'npm ci' installs exact versions from package-lock.json and is faster and more reliable for CI/CD environments.

title: Docker Security Best Practices
text:
Security is critical when running containers in production. A misconfigured container can expose your entire host system. Here are the essential security practices every DevOps engineer must follow.
Container Security Layers
graph TD
    A["🔒 Image Security"] --> A1["Use official base images"]
    A --> A2["Scan for vulnerabilities"]
    A --> A3["Use minimal base (Alpine)"]
    B["👤 Runtime Security"] --> B1["Run as non-root user"]
    B --> B2["Read-only filesystem"]
    B --> B3["Drop capabilities"]
    C["🌐 Network Security"] --> C1["Limit exposed ports"]
    C --> C2["Use internal networks"]
    C --> C3["Never expose Docker socket"]

    style B fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style C fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
Secure Dockerfile Example
FROM node:18-alpine

title: Docker Security Best Practices
text:
# Create a non-root user
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --chown=appuser:appgroup . .
# Switch to non-root user
USER appuser
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

docker scout cves myapp:latest
# Run with read-only filesystem
docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp myapp
# Run with limited capabilities
docker run --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE myapp
# Never do this in production!
docker run -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock  # DANGEROUS!

title: Docker Security Best Practices
text: Never run containers as root in production! If an attacker escapes the container, they'll have root access to your host machine. Always create and switch to a non-root user with the USER directive in your Dockerfile.

title: Container Debugging & Troubleshooting
text:
When containers misbehave in production, you need a systematic approach to diagnose and fix issues. Here's the debugging toolkit every DevOps engineer needs.
Container Debugging Flowchart
graph TD
    START["🚨 Container Problem"] --> Q1{"Is it running?"}
    Q1 -->|No| A1["docker ps -a\nCheck exit code"]
    A1 --> A2["docker logs container_id\nRead error messages"]
    Q1 -->|Yes but unhealthy| B1["docker logs -f container_id\nWatch live logs"]
    B1 --> B2["docker exec -it id sh\nShell into container"]
    B2 --> B3["docker stats\nCheck CPU/Memory"]
    A2 --> FIX["🔧 Fix and Redeploy"]

    style FIX fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
Debugging Commands
# Step 1: Check container status and exit codes
docker ps -a                              # See all containers + exit status

title: Container Debugging & Troubleshooting
text:
# Exit code 0 = normal exit
# Exit code 1 = application error
# Exit code 137 = killed (OOM or SIGKILL)
# Exit code 143 = graceful termination (SIGTERM)
# Step 2: Read logs
docker logs <container_id>                # Full log output
docker logs --tail 50 <container_id>      # Last 50 lines
docker logs -f <container_id>             # Follow logs in real-time
# Step 3: Shell into a running container
docker exec -it <container_id> /bin/sh    # Open interactive shell
# Step 4: Inspect container details
docker inspect <container_id>             # Full JSON config + network info
docker stats                              # Live CPU/Memory/Network usage

title: Container Debugging & Troubleshooting
text:
# Step 5: Debug a crashing container
docker run -it --entrypoint /bin/sh myapp  # Override CMD to get a shell
tip
Pro debugging trick: If a container keeps crashing on startup, override the entrypoint to get a shell: 'docker run -it --entrypoint /bin/sh myapp'. This lets you poke around inside the container's filesystem and run the app manually to see the real error.

title: What is the simplest way to explain a Docker Container vs Image?
text:
Image = The blueprint or recipe (read-only file).
Container = The actual house or dish (running instance).

You can build 100 identical containers from just 1 image!

title: Why are containers faster than Virtual Machines (VMs)?
text:
VMs pack a full operating system (Guest OS) for every app, taking gigabytes and minutes to boot.

Containers share the main computer's OS kernel, taking only megabytes and starting in seconds.

title: What is the difference between CMD and RUN in a Dockerfile?
text:
RUN = Executed while BUILDING the image (e.g. installing software like `npm install`).

CMD = Executed when the container STARTS (e.g. `node server.js`).

ENTRYPOINT = Like CMD but cannot be overridden by command-line arguments (use for the main executable).

title: What does port mapping '-p 8080:80' do in 'docker run'?
text:
It connects host port 8080 to container port 80.

Host Port : Container Port

Now typing http://localhost:8080 on your laptop forwards traffic into port 80 inside the container.

title: What happens to data inside a container when the container is deleted?
text:
Any data stored inside the container's writable layer is permanently lost!

To save data permanently, use Docker Volumes (-v volume_name:/data) or bind mounts.

title: What is a multi-stage Docker build?
text:
A Dockerfile with multiple FROM stages. Stage 1 compiles/builds the app (heavy — includes compilers, dev tools). Stage 2 copies only the built output into a minimal runtime image.

Result: 1.2 GB build stage → 85 MB production image.

Key syntax: COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist

title: What does exit code 137 mean?
text:
137 = 128 + 9 (signal 9 = SIGKILL).

The container was forcefully killed — usually by the Linux OOM (Out of Memory) killer when the container exceeds its memory limit.

Fix: Increase memory limit with --memory flag or optimize the application's memory usage.

title: Why should you never run containers as root?
text:
If an attacker exploits a vulnerability and escapes the container, they'd have ROOT ACCESS to the entire host machine!

Always add a non-root user in your Dockerfile:
RUN adduser -S appuser
USER appuser

unit_title: Enterprise Endpoint Security: EPP, EDR & XDR Defense
title: 1. What is Endpoint Security & Why It Exists
text:
### What is Endpoint Security?
Endpoint security is the process of protecting network endpoints — desktops, laptops, mobile devices, servers, and IoT devices — from malicious threats and cyberattacks. It combines preventative protection (**EPP**) with continuous detection and response capabilities (**EDR**).
According to IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report 2023, the average data breach cost reached **$4.45 million** — a 15% increase over three years.
#### Why Endpoint Security Exists:
- **Expanding Attack Surface**: Remote work and cloud adoption mean devices are no longer perimeter-protected by traditional firewalls.
- **Sophisticated Threats**: Fileless malware, zero-days, and ransomware bypass legacy antivirus.

title: What is Git?
text:
Think of Git as a supercharged 'Time Machine' for your code. Every time you make a checkpoint (called a **commit**), Git saves a snapshot of your entire project. If you break something, you can easily travel back to any previous snapshot.
It also lets multiple software engineers work on the exact same project simultaneously without overwriting each other's work. Git is a **Distributed Version Control System** (DVCS) — every developer has a full copy of the entire project history on their machine.
Git vs GitHub — The Relationship

git init                     # Turn current folder into a Git repository

text:
Git has a unique concept called the **Staging Area** (also called the Index). Think of it like a photography studio: you don't take a photo of your entire house — you choose which items to arrange on the stage, then take the photo (commit).
The Three Areas of Git

Staging and Committing

title: Staging Area and Commits
text:
# Stage specific files
git add index.html             # Stage one file
git add src/                   # Stage entire directory
git add .                      # Stage ALL changes
git add -p                     # Interactive: choose which changes to stage
# Check what's staged
git status                     # See staged vs unstaged files
git diff                       # See unstaged changes
git diff --staged              # See what's about to be committed
# Commit (take the snapshot)
git commit -m "Add login page"           # Commit with a message
git commit -am "Fix typo"                # Stage + commit tracked files
# Undo mistakes
git restore file.txt                     # Discard unstaged changes
git restore --staged file.txt            # Unstage a file (keep changes)

title: Staging Area and Commits
text:
tip
Good commit messages follow this pattern: 'verb + what changed'. Examples: 'Add user login page', 'Fix database connection timeout', 'Remove deprecated API endpoint'. Bad example: 'fixed stuff'.

title: Branching and Merging
text:
A **branch** is like a parallel universe for your project. The main production code lives on the `main` branch. When building a new feature, you create a feature branch so you don't break working code. When the feature is done and tested, you merge it back.
Branch and Merge Workflow
gitGraph
    commit id: "Initial"
    commit id: "Setup"
    branch feature-login
    checkout feature-login
    commit id: "Add form"
    commit id: "Add validation"
    checkout main
    commit id: "Hotfix"
    merge feature-login id: "Merge feature"
    commit id: "Deploy v2"
Branching Commands

title: Branching and Merging
text:
# Create and manage branches
git branch                      # List all local branches
git branch feature-login        # Create a new branch
git checkout feature-login      # Switch to feature-login branch
git checkout -b feature-login   # Shortcut: create AND switch
git switch feature-login        # Modern alternative to checkout
git switch -c feature-login     # Modern: create AND switch
# Merging
git checkout main               # Switch back to main
git merge feature-login         # Merge feature-login INTO main
# Cleanup
git branch -d feature-login     # Delete branch after merge
git branch -D feature-login     # Force delete unmerged branch
info
Naming convention: Use descriptive branch names with prefixes. Examples: feature/user-auth, bugfix/login-crash, hotfix/security-patch, chore/update-deps. This makes branches self-documenting.

title: Resolving Merge Conflicts
text:
A **merge conflict** happens when two branches modify the same line in the same file. Git doesn't know which version to keep, so it asks YOU to resolve it manually. Don't panic — conflicts are normal and are a sign of active collaboration! How Merge Conflicts Happen sequenceDiagram participant M as main participant A as feature-A participant B as feature-B M->>A: Branch off M->>B: Branch off A->>A: Edit line 10: color = blue B->>B: Edit line 10: color = red A->>M: Merge feature-A ✅ B->>M: Merge feature-B ⚠️ CONFLICT! Note over M: Both changed line 10!
Git asks YOU to choose. What a Conflict Looks Like in Your File

title: Resolving Merge Conflicts
text:
<<<<<<< HEAD (your current branch)
color = blue
=======
color = red
>>>>>>> feature-B (the branch being merged)
# To resolve:
# 1. Choose one version, combine them, or write something new
# 2. Remove the <<<, ===, >>> markers
# 3. Save the file
# 4. git add the resolved file
# 5. git commit to complete the merge
Conflict Resolution Commands
# When a merge conflict occurs:
git status                      # See which files have conflicts
# After manually editing the conflicted file:
git add resolved-file.txt       # Mark as resolved
git commit                      # Complete the merge

title: Resolving Merge Conflicts
text:
# Abort if you want to start over:
git merge --abort               # Cancel the merge entirely
# Use a visual merge tool:
git mergetool                   # Opens configured visual diff tool
tip
Interview pro tip: 'I minimize conflicts by keeping feature branches short-lived (merge within 1-2 days), frequently pulling from main to stay updated, and communicating with teammates when we're working on the same files.'

title: Rebase vs Merge
text:
Both `merge` and `rebase` combine work from two branches, but they do it differently. This is one of the most frequently asked Git questions in interviews.
Merge: Preserves Full History
gitGraph
    commit id: "A"
    commit id: "B"
    branch feature
    checkout feature
    commit id: "C"
    commit id: "D"
    checkout main
    commit id: "E"
    merge feature id: "Merge commit"
**Merge** creates a new 'merge commit' that ties both branches together. The history shows exactly when and where the branch diverged and reconnected. It's safe and preserves the full truth of what happened.

title: Rebase vs Merge
text:
**Rebase** replays your feature commits on top of the latest main, creating a clean linear history as if you had started your work from the latest main all along. The history looks cleaner, but it rewrites commit hashes.
When to Use Each
# MERGE — Safe for shared/public branches
git checkout main
git merge feature-login         # Creates a merge commit
# REBASE — Clean history for local/private branches
git checkout feature-login
git rebase main                 # Replay commits on top of main
git checkout main
git merge feature-login         # Now it's a fast-forward (linear)

title: Rebase vs Merge
text:
# Interactive rebase — Squash messy commits before merge
git rebase -i HEAD~3            # Rewrite last 3 commits
# In the editor: change 'pick' to 'squash' to combine commits
warning
Golden Rule: NEVER rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared branch that others are working on. Rebase rewrites commit history, which will cause chaos for teammates who already have the old commits. Only rebase your own local, unpushed work.

title: Git Stash, Tags, and Logs
text:
**Git Stash** is like a clipboard for your code changes. Imagine you're halfway through writing a feature, and your boss says 'Drop everything — fix this critical bug on main!' Stash saves your unfinished work, lets you switch branches cleanly, and restores it later.
Git Stash — Save Work in Progress
# Save current changes to stash
git stash                       # Stash tracked file changes
git stash -u                    # Also stash untracked (new) files
git stash save "WIP: login form"  # Stash with a description

title: Git Stash, Tags, and Logs
text:
# View and restore stashed changes
git stash list                  # List all stashes
git stash pop                   # Restore most recent stash & remove from list
git stash apply                 # Restore stash but keep it in the list
git stash drop stash@{0}        # Delete a specific stash
git stash clear                 # Delete ALL stashes
**Git Tags** mark specific commits as important milestones — like software version releases (v1.0.0, v2.3.1). Tags don't move like branches do; they permanently point to one specific commit.
Git Tags — Version Marking

title: Git Stash, Tags, and Logs
text:
git tag v1.0.0                  # Create a lightweight tag
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First stable release"  # Annotated tag (recommended)
git tag                         # List all tags
git push origin v1.0.0          # Push a specific tag to remote
git push origin --tags          # Push ALL tags to remote
Git Log — Explore History
git log                         # Full commit history
git log --oneline               # Compact one-line format
git log --oneline --graph       # Visual branch graph
git log --author="Alice"        # Filter by author
git log --since="2 weeks ago"   # Filter by date
git show abc1234                # Show details of a specific commit
git blame file.txt              # Show who last modified each line
tip

title: Git Stash, Tags, and Logs
text: git blame is incredibly useful for debugging: 'Who changed this line, when, and in which commit?' It helps you find the context behind a change before you modify it.

title: GitHub Pull Requests and Code Review
text:
A **Pull Request** (PR) is how teams collaborate on GitHub. Instead of pushing directly to main, you push your feature branch and open a PR asking teammates to review your code before merging. Think of it as submitting a homework assignment for your professor to grade before it counts.
Pull Request Workflow

title: GitHub Pull Requests and Code Review
text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant D as Developer
    participant GH as GitHub
    participant R as Code Reviewer
    D->>D: Create feature branch
    D->>D: Write code + commit
    D->>GH: git push origin feature-branch
    D->>GH: Open Pull Request
    GH->>R: Notification: PR ready for review
    R->>GH: Review code + leave comments
    R->>GH: Request changes ❌
    D->>D: Fix issues + push updates
    R->>GH: Approve ✅
    GH->>GH: Merge to main
    GH->>GH: Delete feature branch
PR Workflow from Command Line
# 1. Create and switch to feature branch
git checkout -b feature/user-profile
# 2. Make changes, commit
git add .
git commit -m "Add user profile page with avatar upload"
# 3. Push branch to GitHub
git push origin feature/user-profile

title: GitHub Pull Requests and Code Review
text:
# 4. Open PR on GitHub (or use GitHub CLI)
gh pr create --title "Add user profile page" --body "Implements user profile with avatar upload."
# 5. After PR is approved and merged, clean up
git checkout main
git pull origin main             # Get the merged changes
git branch -d feature/user-profile  # Delete local branch
info
Code review best practices: Keep PRs small (under 400 lines), write descriptive PR titles and descriptions, add screenshots for UI changes, respond to review comments promptly, and test before requesting review.
Keeping Your Branch Updated
# While working on a feature, main may get new commits

title: GitHub Pull Requests and Code Review
text:
# Keep your branch updated to avoid conflicts:
git checkout feature/user-profile
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main           # Replay your commits on latest main
# Or merge main into your branch:
git merge origin/main            # Merge latest main into your branch

title: What are the 3 areas of Git?
text:
1. **Working Directory** — Your actual files on disk (you edit here).
2. **Staging Area (Index)** — Files marked for the next commit (git add puts them here).
3. **Repository (.git)** — Permanent commit history (git commit saves here).

Flow: Working → Staging → Repository

title: What is the difference between Merge and Rebase?
text:
**Merge**: Creates a new 'merge commit' that joins two branches. Preserves complete history including when branches diverged.

**Rebase**: Replays your commits on top of the target branch. Creates a clean, linear history but rewrites commit hashes.

Rule: Rebase local/private branches. Merge shared/public branches.

title: How do you undo the last commit without losing changes?
text:
git reset --soft HEAD~1

This moves HEAD back one commit, but keeps all changes in the staging area. You can re-edit and recommit.

• --soft: Keeps changes staged
• --mixed (default): Keeps changes but unstages them
• --hard: DELETES all changes permanently (dangerous!)

title: What does 'git stash' do?
text:
Temporarily saves your uncommitted changes to a hidden stack, giving you a clean working directory.

Perfect for: 'I need to switch branches but I'm not ready to commit.'

• git stash — Save changes
• git stash pop — Restore and remove from stack
• git stash list — View all stashed items

title: What is a Pull Request (PR)?
text:
A PR is a request to merge your feature branch into main on GitHub/GitLab.

Workflow:
1. Push feature branch to remote
2. Open PR with description of changes
3. Teammates review code and leave comments
4. Fix any issues and push updates
5. After approval, merge to main

PRs enable code review, catching bugs before they reach production.

title: What does 'git cherry-pick' do?
text:
Copies a specific commit from one branch and applies it to your current branch — without merging the entire branch.

Useful when: A critical bugfix was committed on a feature branch, and you need it on main immediately without merging the whole incomplete feature.

Usage: git cherry-pick <commit-hash>

Docker lets you run containers on a single computer. But what happens when you have 500 containers running across 50 servers in the cloud? That's where **Kubernetes** (also called K8s) comes in.
Kubernetes is like the **Captain of a ship** filled with containers. If a container crashes, Kubernetes restarts it. If traffic spikes, Kubernetes scales up extra containers. If a server dies, Kubernetes moves the containers to a healthy server.

A **Pod** is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. It wraps one or more containers that share the same network namespace (same IP address and ports) and storage volumes. Think of a Pod as a tiny apartment — the containers inside share the same address and mailbox.

title: Deployments — Self-Healing & Scaling
text:
A **Deployment** is the most common way to run applications in Kubernetes. It manages a set of identical Pods (called replicas) and provides self-healing: if a Pod crashes, the Deployment automatically creates a replacement. If you need more capacity, just increase the replica count. Deployment Self-Healing sequenceDiagram participant D as Deployment
replicas: 3 participant RS as ReplicaSet participant P1 as Pod 1 ✅ participant P2 as Pod 2 ✅ participant P3 as Pod 3 💀 D->>RS: Ensure 3 replicas running RS->>P1: Running RS->>P2: Running RS->>P3: Crashed! RS->>RS: Detected: only 2/3 running RS->>P3: Auto-create replacement Pod Note over RS,P3: Self-healing complete
3/3 Pods healthy Deployment Manifest

title: Deployments — Self-Healing & Scaling
text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 3                    # Run 3 identical pods
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:                      # Pod template
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.25
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "100m"
              memory: "64Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "200m"
              memory: "128Mi"
Deployment Commands
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml         # Create/update deployment
kubectl get deployments                  # List deployments
kubectl scale deployment web-app --replicas=5  # Scale to 5 pods
kubectl rollout status deployment web-app  # Watch rollout progress
kubectl rollout undo deployment web-app    # Rollback to previous version
tip

title: Deployments — Self-Healing & Scaling
text: Interview question: 'How does Kubernetes achieve self-healing?' Answer: The Deployment controller continuously compares the desired state (3 replicas) with the actual state. If a Pod dies, the controller creates a new one to match the desired state. This is called the 'reconciliation loop'.
